JOURNAL OF L ATEX CLASS FILES, VOL. 1, NO. 1, MAY 2026 1
Load Scheduling for Pulse Charging to Flatten
Aggregate Power Demand
Yu Liu
Abstract—Pulse charging can be used to boost up charging
speed for lithium-ion batteries and delay battery capacity fading
by periodically pausing the current during charging. However,
this technique introduces intermittence for current and may
thus challenge the electric stability of charger as well as its
energy supply source. To deal with this challenge, a coordination
method for multiple loads simultaneously being charged has been
proposed in this paper. The method exploits the off-time intervals
of pulse current to charge other loads. By properly grouping and
coordinating the charging loads, the fluctuation and amplitude of
the charging current can be mitigated. To optimally schedule all
charging loads, mathematical models are formulated to help find
out the best scheduling scheme for the loads. Two scenarios have
been considered as well as two mathematical models have been
proposed and elucidated in the paper. In one scenario all loads
are charged using PCs with the same frequency, while in the other
scenario PCs with various frequencies are considered. In addition,
a procedure of scheduling the charging process considering power
limit is developed. The proposed method has been applied to and
quantitatively evaluated in two application scenarios. Compared
to randomly charging, both fluctuation and amplitude of the
total current for multiple loads simultaneously being charged
have been mitigated after properly scheduled. Using the proposed
method, the merits of pulse charging for batteries can be utilized
while the stability issue can be alleviated.
Index Terms—Electric vehicle, pulse charging, orderly charg-
ing, charging scheduling.

I. INTRODUCTION
ELECTRIC vehicle (EV) sales have exceeded 17 million,
accounting over 20% of all cars sold worldwide in 2024,
and over 40% cars sold globally is predicted to be EV by 2030
[1]. As the EV market is booming, rapidly growing of the
charging demand is expected. EVs consumes about 0.7% of
the world’s total electricity, and this share is expected to reach
2.5% by 2030 [1]. Charging of EVs not only increases the
cumulative power level on electricity grid but also challenges
the grid stability with fast transients [2]. Nevertheless, when
properly coordinated, charging of EVs can also assist to
support the grid through peak shaving, frequency regulation,
voltage profile improvement, congestion management, etc. [3].
Conventional charging techniques for batteries include con-
stant current (CC) charging, constant voltage charging (CV),
and constant current-constant voltage (CC-CV) [4], [5]. For
Li-ion battery (LIB), the CC-CV technique is widely adopted
thanks to its simplicity and easy implementation: the CC-CV
technique keeps the charging current for LIB constant until a
preset voltage of the LIBs is reached, then the charging voltage
is hold constant while the charging current exponentially
decreases, and the charging process ends when a minimum
value of the current is reached [5]. Compared to the CC
technique, the CC-CV technique allows LIBs to be almost
fully charged and avoid overcharge, but it needs more time to
finish the charging process and accelerates the capacity fading
[6].
To boost up the charging velocity, various charging ap-
proaches have been proposed such as Multistage Constant
Current (MCC) technique, which consists of several CC stages
with different current levels. The MMC may limit the capacity
fading and shorten the charging time through reducing gener-
ated heat and mechanical stress within LIBs during charging
[7]. Another fast charging technique called pulse charging,arXiv:2603.29712v1  [eess.SY]  31 Mar 2026

JOURNAL OF L ATEX CLASS FILES, VOL. 1, NO. 1, MAY 2026 2
which offers lower rate of impedance rising compared to the
MCC, has been discussed in literature. In this technique, pulse
current (PC), which is periodically interrupted, is used instead
of continuous current to charge the LIBs. The short pause set
in each period offers a relaxation which can help eliminate
concentration polarization, increase the power transfer rate,
and thus reduce the charging time [8]. This technique has
been claimed to be able to alleviate the capacity fading
due to relaxation process set in this charging technique [9].
The concentration is mitigated when the duration of pulse
wave is in the range of seconds, because pulses shorter than
milliseconds can be buffered by large double-layer capacitance
at the electrode/electrolyte interface [10]. Due to these merits,
different charging systems using pulse charging have been
developed such as presented in [11]–[13].
However, the drastically varying and interrupted current and
power of pulse charging may challenges the electric stability
of the terminal during charging. This issue is critical to the
power supply sources for which steady output power is in
favor. For example, if photovoltaic (PV) panels are used to
supply power for charging the LIBs, the frequently varying PC
may disturb the operation point of the PV panels. In such case,
the charging procedure needs to be carefully designed to deal
with this inherent nature of interruption. To smoothly track the
maximal power point of the PV panels, an circuit topology
for pulse charging has been proposed in [14], in which
two additional batteries are explored to consume the positive
PV power during the charging interruption and the reverse
discharging power of the main battery. The interruption of PC
can be suppressed or even eliminated when multiple batteries
simultaneously being charged are properly coordinated. A
control scheme regulating the buck converters controlling the
pulse charging currents from fuel cell was proposed in [15],
in which several batteries are synergistically being charged
to avoid drastic changing output power of fuel cell. Through
successively charging two batteries using pulse charging, the
magnitude and the variation of the total current used to charge
the batteries can be reduced [16]. To reduce the number of
charger as well as its complexity, a circuit topology as well as
a control scheme are proposed in [17]. By alternately charging
the batteries, the number of chargers needed can be reduced,
too.
Proper scheduling the charging loads offers the potential to
suppress the fluctuation and eliminate the intermittence of the
charging current. However, the scheduling of multiple batteries
using PC remains missing in the current literature. Aiming at
this issue, a method for scheduling multiple batteries being
charged at the same time is developed and presented in this pa-
per with following contributions: First, a concept of adjusting
the waveform of pulse charging current without changing the
charging power is proposed. Second, two mathematical models
and procedures for scheduling multiple loads simultaneously
being charged using PCs with the same frequency and various
frequencies are developed, respectively. Third, a procedure
for coordinating charging loads considering power limit is
proposed.
This paper is organized as follows. Section II presents the
concept of adjusting pulse current for a load without reducingthe charging power. The idea of grouping and shifting the PCs
for multiple loads to reduce the amplitude and fluctuation of
the total current is presented in this section. After that, two
scenarios regarding pulse frequency are considered. For each
scenario, the grouping and shifting problem is mathematically
modeled. Base on the mathematical solution, a procedure of
scheduling the charging loads is developed. The proposed
method is applied to two test simulations. The simulation
results are presented and discussed in section III. Conclusions
are drawn in section IV.
II. OPTIMIZED SCHEDULING OF PULSE CURRENTS
The periodic interruption of current introduced by the pulse
charging offers batteries pauses to uniformly diffuse and
distribute the electrolyte’s ions [17]. However, this causes
undesired intermittence of current and power supply at the
charging terminal. When multiple batteries are being charged
simultaneously, this is commonly the case for the batteries
in a battery pack, such intermittence can be mitigated or even
eliminated through properly coordinating the charging currents
flowing to the batteries. In this section, an optimal coordination
scheme is developed and elucidated in details.
A. The potential of staggering pulses from different currents
The profile of a PC used in pulse charging can be approx-
imately regarded as a sequence which consists of a series of
rectangular pulses as shown in Fig. 1. In a PC, each pulse
occurs at equal intervals within a periodTalong the time
axis, and each period covers a complete on-and-off cycle of a
pulse. During one period, a pulse is active for a time interval
ofton, after that the pulse is inactive for a time intervalt off.
In the on-stage, the charging current flows through a battery,
and the battery will be charged. In the off-stage, the charging
current falls to zero, and the charging process for the battery
is temporally suspended. The ratio oft ontoTis commonly

A single pulse current introduces intermittence not only to
the battery but also to the power supply source such as utility
grid. This may pose a challenge to the stability of the power
supply source, and this issue needs to be carefully dealt with.
Nevertheless, when multiple batteries are charged using pulse
charging at the same time, it is possible to adjust the PCs to
eliminate this inherent intermittence. The idea is to shift the
phases of each PC, so that the pulses from one PC can appear
in the off-intervals of another PC. It should be noted that, in

B. Adjusting the waveform of pulse current
As discussed above, it is possible to avoid the occurrence of
pulses from two PCs at the same time by adjusting their initial
phases. The condition, i.e. the pulse width of any PC is not
greater than the off-interval of the other PC, must be satisfied.
However, if this condition is not met, the waveforms of the PCs
need to be adjusted. The adjustment can be implemented by
tuning the period, the duty ratio, or/and the amplitude. To keep
the frequency constant, only the duty ratio and the amplitude
are changed here. An example of decreasing the duty ratio
and increasing the amplitude without changing the period is
shown in Fig. 3.

C. Arranging pulse currents having the same frequency
The potential and precondition for shifting PCs to avoid the
overlap of multiple pulses have been discussed in the previous
section. Note that the PCs may have different frequencies. To
begin with, this section focuses on the shifting of PCs at the
same frequency as a simpler case. It is considered thatN c
batteries are being charged using pulse charging at the same
time. All PCs have the same frequency and amplitude, while
the duty ratios may not necessarily identical to each other.
Taking two PCs marked 1 and 2 as an example, if the pulse
width of PC2is not greater than the off-interval of PC 1, i.e.
ton,2≤toff,1, the pulse from PC2can be shifted into the off-
intervalt off,1, as shown in Fig. 4. Consequently, the overlap
between the pulses from PC1and PC2is avoided.
If the remaining part oft off,1 after subtractingt on,2 is not
smaller than the pulse width from another PCx, i.e.t off,1−
ton,2≥ton,x, the pulse from PCxcan also be shifted into
the intervalt off,1 to stagger the pulses from PC 1 and 2, as
shown in Fig. 4. Generally, for a group of PCs at the same
frequency, if the sum of the pulse widths from PC 2 to PCx
is not greater than the off-interval of PC 1, it is possible to
shift the pulses from thesex−1PCs into the off-interval of
PC 1 to avoid overlap between the pulses.
To mitigate the intermittence and fluctuation in the total
charging current of multiple batteries,i Σ, the pulses from
different PCs need to be uniformly distributed along the time

A pulse to be shifted can analogized as an item, while the
off-interval can be regarded as a bin. Each item has a size
determined by its pulse width, and each bin has a capacity
corresponding to its time duration, as illustrated in Fig. 5.
Accordingly, the problem of optimally shifting the pulses can
be mapped to the classic bin packing problem, which aims to
pack items of varying sizes into bins with fixed and predefined
capacities, such that the number of bins used is minimized
[18]. For simplicity reason, the PCs to be shifted are treated
as items, and the off-intervals are treated as bins in this paper.
To avoid double counting, each pulse is allowed to be assigned
to at most one off-interval of another PC.

Since all PCs operate at the same frequency and the pulses
repeat within the same time period, it is sufficient to considerthe problem for a single period. Thus, for each PC, only one
representative pulse and its corresponding off-interval need
to be considered. To mathematically formulate the grouping
problem, several variables are introduced. The variablex iis
used to indicate whether PCiis treated as bin-type or item-
type. Whenx i= 1, PCiis treated as bin-type, and pulses from
other PCs can be shifted into its off-interval. Otherwise,x i= 0
indicates that PCiis treated as item-type, and the pulses from
PCican be scheduled to turn on during the off-intervals
of a bin-type PC. To describe the grouping relationship, an
additional variabley ijis utilized to indicate whether the pulse
from PCjcan be shifted to the off-interval of PCi. If the pulse
from PCjcan be shifted to the off-interval of PCiwithout
overlapping with the pulse of PCi,y ij= 1; otherwisey ij= 0.
For a real bin packing problem, if all items can be packed,
it is obvious that fewer bins means less unused space in the
bins. Determining a scheme to pack all items using the fewest
bins is equivalent to minimizing the remaining space in the
bins. Analogously, intermittence can be viewed as a form of
unused space within the off-intervals. Therefore, to eliminate
the intermittence, the off-intervals should be filled with pulses
that can be shifted. If all pulses from the item-type PCs can
be shifted to the off-intervals of the bin-type PCs, fewer bin-
type PCs results in fewer unfilled off-intervals and thus less
intermittence. Therefore, the optimal scheme for shifting the
currents is consistent with minimizing the number of bin-type
PCs. ForN cbatteries, this objective can be mathematically
expressed as:

These PCs are grouped together as groupi, where PCiis the

D. Arranging PCs having various frequencies
In some cases, different batteries may be charged using
PCs operating at different frequencies to minimize the battery
impedance, since batteries have different internal resistance
[11]. The duty ratios of different PCs are not equal to each
other and may also vary with time [19]. In this section, PCs
operating at different frequencies are considered. To mitigate
the intermittency and fluctuation in the total charging current
for multiple batteries, which are being charged using PCs at
various frequencies, a grouping and pulse-shifting scheme is
developed and explained in this section.
A set of PCs operating at different frequencies and duty
ratios is illustrated by the profiles in Fig. 6. Since the pulses
from different PCs may occur at different times, the relative
positions of pulses and off-intervals from different PCs on the
time axis are not fixed. Therefore, shifting the pulses from
a PC to the off-intervals of another PC on the time axis is
feasible only if the following two conditions are satisfied.
First, there exists at least one PC whose pulse width is less
than or equal to the off-interval of at least one other PC in
the group. This condition is straightforward: if the width of
every pulse is greater than all off-intervals in the group, then
it is impossible to shift any pulse into an off-interval without
causing overlap of pulses. Second, for any two PCs that satisfy
the first condition, their periods must be such that the larger
period is an integer multiple of the smaller one. This condition
ensures that if a pulse from PCacan be shifted to an off-
interval of PCb, then all pulses from PCacan also be shifted
to the off-intervals of PCb.
Once both conditions are satisfied, all pulses in the group
can be scheduled to avoid overlap. Similarly, the grouping and
shifting problem can be analogized to the bin packing problem.

Similar to the previous case, to eliminate the intermittence

achieve these two goals, a strategy for grouping the PCs and
scheduling their phases must be designed.

IV. CONCLUSIONS
To mitigate the fluctuation and intermittence of current
for multiple loads simultaneously being charged using pulse
charging method, a method for coordinating the charging
process for the loads has been proposed in this paper. First,
the concept of adjusting pulse current without changing the
charging power was introduced. Then the potential of ex-
ploiting the off-time intervals of pulse current to charge other
loads was explained. Through properly grouping the loads and
shifting the charging currents on the time axis, the current
pulses can be staggered. Thereafter, to find out the optimal

charging scheme for all loads, the scheduling problem was
mathematically described. Two scenarios were considered and
two correspondent mathematical models have been proposed.
In one scenario all loads are charged using PCs with the
same frequency, and in the other scenario PCs with various
frequencies are used. In addition, a procedure of scheduling
the charging process considering power limit is developed.
The proposed method has been applied to and quantitatively
evaluated in two application scenarios. Compared to randomly
charging, both fluctuation and amplitude of the total current for
multiple loads simultaneously being charged have been mit-
igated after properly scheduled. Using the proposed method,
the merits of pulse charging for batteries can be utilized while
the challenge to stability of electric power supply can be
addressed.

structure.title: Preface
structure.summary:
This partial document discusses a method for load scheduling in pulse charging of lithium-ion batteries to flatten aggregate power demand. The main points covered are:

*   **Problem:** Pulse charging, while beneficial for battery speed and longevity, introduces intermittent current that can destabilize power sources.
*   **Proposed Solution:** A coordination method for multiple loads being pulse-charged simultaneously. This method utilizes the off-time intervals of one load's pulse charging to charge other loads.
*   **Key Contributions:**
    *   Concept of adjusting pulse charging waveform without reducing charging power.
    *   Development of two mathematical models for scheduling loads with same and various pulse frequencies.
    *   A procedure for coordinating charging loads while considering power limits.
*   **Methodology:** The paper formulates mathematical models to find optimal scheduling schemes. It considers two scenarios: all loads using pulse charging with the same frequency, and loads using pulse charging with various frequencies.
*   **Benefits:** By properly grouping and coordinating charging loads, the fluctuation and amplitude of the total charging current can be mitigated, thus alleviating stability issues while still leveraging the advantages of pulse charging.
*   **Evaluation:** The proposed method is applied and quantitatively evaluated in two application scenarios, showing significant mitigation of current fluctuation and amplitude compared to random charging.
*   **Context:** The introduction highlights the booming electric vehicle market and the associated challenges and opportunities for the electricity grid. It also reviews conventional and advanced battery charging techniques, including pulse charging and its benefits and drawbacks.

structure.title: OPTIMIZED SCHEDULING OF PULSE CURRENTS
structure.summary: This partial document discusses the challenges and solutions related to pulse charging of Lithium-ion batteries (LIBs). It highlights the benefits of pulse charging, such as reduced impedance rise and faster charging times, by allowing for relaxation periods that mitigate concentration polarization. However, it also points out the issue of electric instability at the power supply terminal due to the interrupted nature of pulse charging, especially when using sources like photovoltaic panels. The document then delves into existing approaches to address this, including using additional batteries or coordinating multiple batteries to smooth out power fluctuations. The paper's main contribution is a proposed method for scheduling multiple batteries being charged simultaneously using pulse currents. This method involves adjusting the pulse charging waveform without altering the charging power, and it includes mathematical models for scheduling with same and various pulse frequencies, as well as a procedure for coordinating loads under power limits. The document outlines the structure of the paper, with Section II detailing the concept of optimizing pulse current scheduling by staggering pulses from different charging currents to reduce amplitude and fluctuation.

nodes.title: The potential of staggering pulses from different currents
nodes.summary:
This partial document discusses the challenges and solutions related to pulse charging of Lithium-ion batteries (LIBs), particularly when multiple batteries are charged simultaneously.

The main points covered are:

*   **Benefits of Pulse Charging (PC):** PC offers advantages over continuous current charging, including lower impedance rise, reduced charging time, and alleviation of capacity fading due to relaxation periods.
*   **Challenges of PC for Power Sources:** The interrupted and varying nature of PC can destabilize power supply sources like photovoltaic panels or fuel cells, requiring careful design to maintain steady output.
*   **Mitigation Strategies for Intermittency:** The document explores methods to suppress or eliminate the intermittency of PC when charging multiple batteries. This includes:
    *   **Coordinating charging of multiple batteries:** Using additional batteries or fuel cells to absorb power fluctuations.
    *   **Successive charging:** Charging batteries sequentially to reduce the magnitude and variation of total current.
    *   **Alternating charging:** Reducing the number of chargers and complexity by alternately charging batteries.
*   **Proposed Contributions of the Paper:** The paper aims to address the missing aspect of scheduling multiple batteries using PC. Its contributions include:
    *   A concept for adjusting PC waveforms without changing charging power.
    *   Mathematical models and procedures for scheduling multiple loads with the same and various PC frequencies.
    *   A procedure for coordinating charging loads considering power limits.
*   **Optimized Scheduling of Pulse Currents:**
    *   **Staggering pulses:** The core idea is to shift the phases of individual PCs so that pulses from one battery fall within the off-intervals of another, thereby smoothing the total current.
    *   **Adjusting PC waveform:** If direct staggering isn't possible, the duty ratio and amplitude of PCs can be adjusted to satisfy staggering conditions while maintaining charging power.
    *   **Arranging PCs with the same frequency:** This section models the problem as a bin packing problem, where off-intervals are bins and pulses are items to be packed, aiming to minimize the number of "bin-type" PCs (those whose off-intervals are used for other pulses).
    *   **Arranging PCs with various frequencies:** This extends the bin packing analogy to PCs with different frequencies, considering the least common multiple (LCM) of their periods and the conditions required for pulse shifting.

nodes.title: Constraint 1.2
nodes.summary:
The provided document excerpt discusses a method for grouping and scheduling pulses from Power Converters (PCs) to ensure continuous charging current and avoid overlaps.

The main points covered are:

*   **Constraint 1.2:** This constraint ensures that each pulse can be assigned to at most one off-interval, preventing conflicts. It differentiates between "item-type" PCs (whose pulses are shifted) and "bin-type" PCs (whose off-intervals are used for shifting).
*   **Grouping Scheme for Same Frequency PCs:** A method is described to determine a grouping scheme for PCs operating at the same frequency. This involves identifying bin-type PCs and the item-type PCs that will have their pulses shifted to the bin-type PC's off-intervals.
*   **Arranging PCs with Various Frequencies:** The document then addresses the more complex scenario where PCs operate at different frequencies and duty ratios.
*   **Conditions for Pulse Shifting with Various Frequencies:** Two crucial conditions are outlined for successful pulse shifting between PCs with different frequencies:
    1.  The pulse width of at least one PC must be less than or equal to the off-interval of at least one other PC.
    2.  For any two PCs satisfying the first condition, their periods must be such that the larger period is an integer multiple of the smaller one.
*   **Analogy to Bin Packing:** The problem of scheduling pulses from PCs operating at different frequencies is analogized to the bin packing problem. Off-intervals are treated as bins, and pulses are treated as items to be packed.
*   **Objective for Various Frequencies:** The goals are to fill off-intervals as much as possible to eliminate intermittency and to adjust pulse positions to minimize fluctuations in the total charging current.
*   **Mathematical Model Formulation:** The document indicates that a mathematical model is being developed to address this problem.

nodes.title: Arranging PCs having various frequencies
nodes.summary:
The document discusses methods for grouping and scheduling pulses from Pulse Chargers (PCs) to avoid overlaps and ensure efficient charging. It covers two main scenarios: PCs operating at the same frequency and PCs operating at different frequencies.

For PCs at the same frequency, a mathematical model is presented to determine a grouping scheme. This involves identifying "bin-type" PCs that provide off-intervals and "item-type" PCs whose pulses need to be shifted. Constraints ensure that each pulse is shifted to at most one off-interval and that bin-type PCs only provide off-intervals without contributing their own pulses for relocation.

When PCs operate at different frequencies, the problem becomes more complex. Two conditions must be met for pulse shifting to be feasible: the pulse width must be less than or equal to an off-interval, and the periods of PCs must be such that the larger period is an integer multiple of the smaller one. The least common multiple (LCM) of their periods is considered for analysis. The problem is analogized to bin packing, where off-intervals are bins and pulses are items. A mathematical model is formulated with variables indicating PC types, pulse shifting feasibility, and specific off-interval assignments. The objective is to minimize the number of bin-type PCs.

A procedure is also outlined for grouping PCs with different frequencies, starting with the highest frequency PC and then finding other PCs whose frequencies are integral multiples.

Finally, the document addresses coordinating charging loads considering power limits. This involves dividing batteries into groups based on their state-of-charge (SOC) and adjusting charging power (amplitude or duty ratio) if the total power exceeds a maximum limit. If the total power is below the limit, more batteries can be added to the charging group.
